terms.gloss: recite, say back (a lesson, a poem) from memory
evidence: Hor. Ep. 1.18.13–14: puerum … dictāta magistrō reddere
Cic. Brut. 301: ea sine scrīptō verbīs eīsdem redderet
terms.comment: The schoolboy says back to the master what has been dictated to him: dictāta reddere. To make plain that it is from memory, add memoriter (Cic. Lael. 1, Lewis & Short): carmen memoriter reddere.

terms.gloss: recite; read out to an audience
evidence: Hor. Ars 438: Quīntiliō sī quid recitārēs
terms.comment: Classically to read out a text, a law, or one’s own poems to listeners (see read aloud); from memory in Celsus, of patients made to say what they remember (Lewis & Short). Traupman’s word for recite; a recitation is recitātiō (Traupman 31).

phrases.latin: ut puerum saevō crēdās dictāta magistrō reddere vel partīs mīmum tractāre secundās
phrases.english: that you would think it a boy saying his lessons back to a stern master, or a mime playing the second part

phrases.latin: Reddenda est memoriter hesterna lēctiō, satis prōlixa. Vereor ut possim.
phrases.english: We have to recite yesterday’s lesson by heart, and it’s a long one. I’m afraid I can’t.
phrases.source: Erasm. Coll., Euntēs in lūdum litterārium
